text: Three of us, one client, ten weeks. The client is Sunil Kaushal, chair of INZBC.

name: TextBox 1
text: THE PROBLEM

name: TextBox 2
text: Staff do the same work every morning
textPreview: Staff do the same work every morning

name: TextBox 3
text:
INZBC is volunteer-run. A handful of people read the same news sources, answer the same FTA tariff questions, and draft the same member communications by hand.

The quality of what reaches members depends on who did it that day.

The council did not ask for an AI that writes things.
They asked for software that takes the repetitive middle of the work — and never puts an unchecked claim in front of a member.

text: Lead with the problem, not the technology. The constraint is the interesting part.

name: TextBox 1
text: WHAT WE BUILT

name: TextBox 2
text: One application, four modules

name: TextBox 3
text:
Strategic Intelligence Platform — turns public news into an approved daily brief
FTA Explainer — answers tariff questions from a sourced corpus, with citations
Communications Assistant — drafts member content for a named human approver
Member Portal — member-facing shell; membership stays in Member Jungle

One FastAPI backend. One PostgreSQL database. One React application.

name: TextBox 1
text: THE DESIGN IDEA

name: TextBox 2
text: The system refuses rather than guesses
textPreview: The system refuses rather than guesses

name: TextBox 3
text:
A brief cannot be distributed unless a named reviewer approved it, the CEO ruled Continue, and no critical QA failure is open.
The analyst who wrote a brief cannot record its QA result — checked against recorded acts, not job titles, so it holds when one person wears several hats.
The audit log cannot be edited. Fifteen triggers refuse UPDATE and DELETE; the application role is granted INSERT and SELECT only.
Distribution is off by default. So is CORS. A missing redaction policy refuses the call.

One file in ~10,000 lines calls a model provider. The FTA Explainer calls none.

name: TextBox 1
text: A DECISION, AND ITS PAYOFF

name: TextBox 2
text: Why PostgreSQL, and why it mattered
textPreview: Why PostgreSQL, and why it mattered

name: TextBox 3
text:
We compared PostgreSQL against MongoDB. The argument for a document store is schema flexibility. The argument against, here, is that our hardest requirements are constraint-shaped.

A run must not sit in a state its decisions do not justify. A report version must not be submitted before it was created. One line of SQL each — application code everywhere else.

The payoff, months later: an end-to-end test started failing intermittently. The CHECK constraint submitted_at >= created_at was refusing rows. The constraint was right — the host clock and the database container clock were 0.44 seconds apart, so records really were dated after they were stored.

We chose the database that could refuse. It refused something real.

text: This is the independent-research slide. Alternatives, the constraint that decided it, and evidence the decision paid off.

name: TextBox 1
text: HONESTY

name: TextBox 2
text: What we got wrong

name: TextBox 3
text:
Four controls existed, were tested, and were never reachable. Specification said the rule existed; a test asserted it; the enforcing code was never called. We had built reassurance.
→ Now a conformance test refuses to merge any route with no declared authority.

A content hash covered an empty digest regardless of what the analyst selected — and still produced a valid-looking hash. Silent, and the hash is the whole record of what was submitted.

One test flake, two wrong diagnoses. Rate-limiter state, then database pollution. Both fitted the symptoms. Neither was the cause.

Every one of these was quiet. That is the lesson we are taking out of Studio 5.

text: Do not skip this slide. The failures are more convincing than the features.

name: TextBox 1
text: OUTCOME

name: TextBox 2
text: Where it stands

name: TextBox 3
text:
Released as v1.0.0. Five of six objectives achieved.
The sixth — production deployment — was deliberately not attempted. It is INZBC's decision and it has not been made. production_enabled is false.

What is ready: one command brings the system up on a clean machine; versioned migrations that refuse to run against a database they do not match; operator, incident and recovery guides.
What is not: the system has been tested, not used. No brief has been produced on a Tuesday morning when someone needed it.

name: TextBox 1
text: RECOMMENDATIONS

name: TextBox 2
text: What we would do next

name: TextBox 3
text:
1. Close the four open decisions with INZBC. Everything about deployment waits on them.
2. Run one real brief end to end with staff, in a working week, before enabling anything.
3. Add a second reviewer account. The separation-of-duties control already supports it — no code change needed.
4. Commission an independent accessibility audit before the public site goes live.
5. Keep writing the decision records. They are cheap to maintain and expensive to reconstruct.

2. Brief Builder loads that run's own candidates and its recorded source coverage
3. CEO Decision: "Not reachable yet — this run is currently Report Drafted. The CEO decision opens once QA has passed."

That refusal is the state machine enforcing itself against the database.
It is the whole argument of the project in one screen.
